paper_title: S-Agent 2.0: Spatial Reasoning with a General Coding Agent

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Spatial reasoning asks a model to work out where objects are in 3D space, how they relate to one another, and how they move. Agentic VLMs have recently brought large improvements on such tasks by letting the model actively gather evidence with 3D perception tools instead of answering in a single pass. Even so, on many questions the tools return the right evidence and the model still does not arrive at the correct answer: the gap between model and tools, where raw readings become usable conclusions, is left unfilled. We present S-Agent 2.0, a spatial reasoning agent that equips an off-the-shelf general coding agent with a command-line perception toolkit, and we design the interface around one principle: help the VLM close the evidence loop: acquire scene evidence, remember it in a persistent scene memory, and interpret each reading in plain spatial language. This design keeps the full flexibility of a coding agent, and every reading it acts on stays grounded in the tools' geometry. On MMSI-Bench and ReVSI, the toolkit improves a strong open-source model, Qwen3.8-27B, by +13.9 and +20.5 points over the same agent without tools, and a strong closed-source model, Gemini-3.8-Flash, by +11.2 and +9.6 points. With the open backbone S-Agent 2.0 reaches 66.5 on MMSI-Bench and 82.3 on ReVSI, ahead of the specialized system SpatialClaw on the same backbone (62.6 and 74.5), and with Gemini-3.8-Flash it reaches 74.1 and 90.5 against its 67.0 and 79.7. Both tool gains shrink as the backbone grows more capable, but SpatialClaw's shrinks far more on ReVSI, from +13.2 to +2.7, while ours stays at +9.6. S-Agent 2.0 also works across different general coding agent harnesses, such as Codex and Claude Code.

Introduction Spatial intelligence, the ability to understand where things are, how they relate in three dimensions, and how the world would look as one moves through it, is foundational to visual perception [6, 40] and essential for any agent that operates in the physical world [12, 2, 30, 15, 3]. Agentic VLMs such as S-Agent [11] have recently brought large improvements here: instead of answering in single pass, the model actively gathers evidence with 3D perception tools while it reasons [23, 7]. More recent work such as SpatialClaw [10] responds with specialized harness: custom state machine that drives the VLM through hand-designed loop (plan, act, reflect) over persistent code kernel with library of 3D perception and geometry utilities, leveraging the flexibility of code to bridge the gap. Even so, on many questions the tools return the right evidence and the model still does not arrive at the correct answer (see Figure 4). Watching such system work reveals where it actually fails. spatial answer is grounded only when complete evidence loop closes: acquire the measurement, remember it while the rest of the evidence is gathered, and interpret the reading into understanding. Specialized systems invest almost entirely in acquisition, in the form of ever richer perception and geometry libraries, and leave the other two steps to the model. In our analysis of SpatialClaw trajectories, acquisition is rarely what breaks. The failures come in two forms. In the first, the model misreads reading it holds: it flips the sign of rotation it measured correctly, or reads correct number in the wrong coordinate frame or the wrong sense. In the second, the evidence never reaches the answer at all: the measurement sits in the workspace while the model eyeballs the pictures, or correct reading is discarded for an unrelated stated reason. The second form exposes break between collecting evidence and drawing the conclusion. Once the readings are in, the reasoning that produces the answer runs detached from them, and the model falls back on its own perception of the scene. On the surface only interpretation goes wrong; underneath, the evidence that was acquired is never fully used. Closing the loop therefore places requirement on each step. Acquisition has to combine easily with the VLMs own perception, so that what the model recognizes and what the tools measure enter the same scene. Acquired evidence needs memory that holds it without effort, so that it stays within reach until the answer is written. And interpretation needs spatial language, so that reading arrives in the terms the question is asked in. 2 1.1. S-Agent 2.0 S-Agent 2.0 is our answer to those requirements: spatial reasoning agent assembled from stock general-purpose coding agent [25, 1, 36] and command-line perception toolkit designed to meet them. General-purpose coding agents (the harnesses behind modern software-engineering agents) already provide the scaffolding spatial reasoner needs (a shell, file system, code execution, long-horizon context management, mature tool-calling loop), and two of their habits bear directly on the requirements above. First, looking at frame or at segmentation mask is an ordinary file view in the agents stream, so the models own look at the scene and the tools readouts interleave in one conversation, with no separate image channel between them.[41] Second, coding agent inspects and revises by reflex: it views an output, corrects what is wrong, and runs again. [41, 16, 29] Applied to scene, that reflex is what joins the two kinds of perception, since the models own perception is checked against what the tools registered before any reading is taken. What these agents lack is perception itself; we keep the harness stock and add it as commands. The design effort goes into the toolkit, which meets the three requirements one by one. Concretely, (i) acquisition combines two kinds of perception, the tools measurements and the models own: the model can register what it perceives or imagines as instances in the scene and drop what the tools got wrong, so both kinds land on one geometric footing; (ii) everything measured persists in scene memory that later steps query by name instead of re-perceiving, so acquired evidence stays within reach until the answer is written; and (iii) every measurement comes back as an answer-ready reading stated in plain spatial language with its interpretation attached. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: We build spatial reasoning agent from stock general-purpose coding agent and commandline perception toolkit, and show that the method works across different general coding agent harnesses (3.3). We design command-line perception toolkit that closes the evidence loop for the agent: each call acquires scene evidence, writes it into persistent scene memory, and returns its reading already interpreted in spatial language, and the models own perception is grounded in the same scene (2). S-Agent 2.0 delivers strong performance. On MMSI-Bench and ReVSI, the perception toolkit adds +13.9 and +20.5 points over the same agent without tools, on the already strong Qwen3.8-27B backbone (3.2), and S-Agent 2.0 surpasses the state-of-the-art agentic spatial reasoning method, whose tool gain on ReVSI shrinks far more on the stronger frontier model Gemini-3.8-Flash while ours remains substantial (3.3). 1.2. Takeaways 1. The method works across coding-agent harnesses. S-Agent 2.0 works across coding-agent harnesses, including OpenHands [36], Codex [25] and Claude Code [1] (3.3). 2. The coding agents inspect-and-revise habit joins the models perception with the tools. The model registers what it perceives or imagines into the scene memory, drops what the tools got wrong (2.3), and cross-checks the memory against the perception outputs (3.4). 3. The remaining gap is model-to-tool grounding. The models reasoning is mostly right; what remains is grounding the question into measurement, which fails in two classes (3.4). 3 2. Method The diagnosis of 1 turns into three requirements that system must meet to close the evidence loop, beyond merely possessing tools. Acquisition joined with the models own perception: what the model recognizes and what the tools measure must enter one scene. Persistent memory: evidence gathered at one step must remain intact and addressable many steps later, without the model carrying it through its own context. Interpretation on arrival: measurement should arrive in the spatial language the question is asked in. Existing systems supply acquisition generously, offering Turing-complete kernel over perception and geometry libraries, but they keep the models own perception in separate channel and leave memory and interpretation to the model. S-Agent 2.0 inverts that allocation: we use general coding agent as the spatial agent, and the design effort moves into tool interface that joins the two kinds of perception and carries memory and interpretation itself. Deciding what to measure is semantic work that VLMs do well, such as identifying which objects the question is about and phrasing segmentation prompt. We build the division into the interface along these two write routes into the scene memory. Tool perception (Ttool) carries the measurement side. The recon command fuses all frames into one metric, gravity-aligned scene and registers every camera in the scene memory; the segment command grounds objects to pixels, taking the models own words as prompts, so deciding what to look for remains semantic work. Model perception (Tmodel) enters through the add-instance command, which grounds the models high-level understanding itself. The model names the new instance, such as an object it recognizes or an observer the question imagines, and initializes its position and pose from other named instances or from pixel locations in the images. The toolkit then treats it like any other instance, so construct that exists only in the models reading of the question is measured on the same geometric footing as the instances that tool perception grounds. The same route also runs in reverse: with drop the model removes an instance the tools registered wrongly, such as mask on reflection, so its own look at the tool perception outputs corrects the memory before any reading is taken from it. Figure 3 shows model perception and tool perception apart in one episode. Detailed descriptions of toolkit interfaces are given in Appendix B. 2.4. The language surface: numbers interpreted on arrival With acquisition routine and memory kept by the environment, the remaining break point is how reading is consumed. Even when the measurement itself is correct, the model may take it in the wrong reference frame, invert which object it is measured from, or ignore it entirely. displacement vector alone does not say which object it points from, whether its axes follow gravity or the camera, or which answer option it favors. That knowledge lives outside the numbers, and the side that computed the geometry holds it most reliably. In previous toolaugmented systems [10], tool calls return bare values or arrays, leaving the whole step from number to usable spatial statement to the model. In the failures we observed, the model calls the right tool and the tool returns the right geometry, yet the final answer still comes out wrong. 6 We therefore have every reply interpret its own numbers, handing the model the values and their plain-language reading together. Each command distills its full output m, against the scene memory S, into compact structured report operc = cτ(m; S), (4) with fixed anatomy: few typed numeric fields with units, together with conclusion, one sentence that restates the measurement in plain spatial language. The conclusion names the entities involved, declares the frame it speaks in (gravity-aligned, camera, or image plane), and carries the reading all the way to the ordinary spatial vocabulary an answer is written in. Figure 3 gives an example: the responses describe relation in words first and keeps the numerical fields that support it, so the model can act on reading without re-deriving it. And the complete measurements and geometry stay in the full output on disk, where the model can read them through the same CLI when it needs them. Together these commitments close the evidence loop. The dashed returns close the loop: the model reads each reply back into its evidence and into the arguments of the next call. 3. Experiments 3.1. Setup Benchmarks. We evaluate S-Agent 2.0 on five benchmarks covering multi-view and video spatial reasoning. For multi-view reasoning, MMSI-Bench [44] provides multiple images of the same scene and tests whether models integrate evidence across views for positional relationships, geometric attributes, motion, and multi-step reasoning; MindCube [34] probes the spatial mental model built from few sparse views, asking for relations the given views never show directly; SPAR-Bench [49] (used for the harness-swap study) spans hierarchy of spatial capabilities from basic metric perception to multi-view relational reasoning. For video reasoning, ReVSI [51] evaluates 3D spatial reasoning from dynamic observations, emphasizing relations that no isolated frame reliably shows; MMSI-Video-Bench [21] extends the MMSI setting to long videos, with questions on spatial construction, motion understanding, cross-video memory, and route planning. ReVSI and SPAR-Bench scores follow the official protocols, macro-averaged over question types; the others report overall accuracy. Models. We use Qwen3.8-27B (FP8, served locally) as the primary backbone; Gemini-3.8Flash as the stronger backbone for the capability study. The general coding agent harness is OpenHands [36] unless stated otherwise, and the same workspaces and toolkit also run under Codex and Claude Code (3.3). The perception tools are served by off-the-shelf models, all frozen: Depth Anything 3 [20] for the metric reconstruction, π3 mos [37, 54] for per-pixel motion masks, GeoCalib [32] for the gravity direction, and SAM 3 [5] for promptable segmentation. 7 Table 1 MMSI-Bench results by question category (C/O/R denote camera/object/region).

Table 6 removes one commitment of 2 at time and leaves the rest of the system untouched. The memory closes the loop only if what it holds is right, and the agent checks that itself. It compares what it sees in perception output against what the registry holds and edits the memory when the two disagree (Figure 4, top right): it drops instances the output shows to be wrong, and keeps suspected duplicate once the output shows genuine second object. The habit is the coding agents inspect-and-revise loop applied to the scene, and it is what joins the models perception with the tools before any reading is taken. What is left is grounding. With acquisition, memory and interpretation carried by the interface, the errors that remain sit where the question first enters the loop (Takeaway 3, Figure 4, bottom right). The agent fails to simulate an imagined viewpoint the question requires, registering an observer with borrowed heading, or it measures the right quantity in the wrong sense, reading an objects elevation above the floor where the question asks for the objects own height. 4. Conclusion We built spatial reasoning agent from stock general coding agent and command-line perception toolkit that closes the evidence loop for the model, joining the tools measurements with the models own perception, keeping every reading in persistent scene memory, and returning each reading interpreted in spatial language. Related Work Spatial reasoning in vision-language models. Spatial competence remains one of the weaker abilities of vision-language models [6, 9, 30], and most of the response has been to put the capability into the weights. One line distills 3D annotations into spatial instruction data at scale, as in SpatialVLM [6], SpatialRGPT [9], Cambrian-S [43], and SenseNova-SI [4]. second line reshapes the backbone itself with geometry-aware modelling or spatially targeted tuning, as in Spatial-MLLM [38] and VST [42]. third line shapes the training signal through reinforcement learning, verifiable rewards, or curricula, as in SpaceR [26], ViLaSR [39], MindCube [34], and SpatialLadder [19]. These models answer in single forward pass out of what training left in their parameters, taking no measurement of the scene in front of them, so new perception backend or shifted task distribution asks for another round of training. S-Agent 2.0 leaves the backbone untouched and moves the work to inference time, where the agent acquires scene evidence on demand and every reading it acts on stays grounded in the tools geometry. Tool-augmented visual agents and code as action. Tool-use agents interleave reasoning with calls to external modules, following the template that ReAct [46] set on the language side. On the visual side, VisProg [17] and ViperGPT [31] synthesize whole program in one pass and then execute it, while MM-ReAct [45], HuggingGPT [28], and OctoTools [22] dispatch requests turn by turn through structured tool menu, and PyVision [53] writes its tooling as it goes. CodeAct [35] compared action formats directly and found executable code to work better than JSON or free text for general-purpose agents, which is the format coding agent uses natively. The tools all of these systems reach for target 2D recognition, so their controllers are never asked to hold metric 3D scene across views and time, which is what spatial question demands. Agentic spatial reasoning. recent line brings tool use to spatial questions. VADAR [24] synthesizes task-specific Pythonic API and then program over it, and pySpatial [23] composes reconstruction, camera-pose recovery, and novel-view synthesis into 3D visual program. GCA [8] splits the model into part that formalizes the question as geometric constraints and part that executes tool calls within them, RieMind [27] queries an explicit 3D scene graph through typed geometric operations, and SpaceTools [7] fine-tunes VLM to coordinate fixed tool set through supervised demonstrations followed by interactive reinforcement learning. Think3D [52] selects camera viewpoints, renders reconstructed point cloud from them, and reasons over the rendered images. Closest to us, S-Agent [11] schedules 3D operations across the views and time steps of multi-view sets and long videos, and SpatialClaw [10] drives the VLM through hand-designed plan, act, and reflect loop over persistent code kernel stocked with 3D perception and geometry utilities. What these systems share is controller written for the purpose and design effort spent on acquisition, on ever richer perception and geometry libraries, while remembering and interpreting the evidence is left to the model and the models own perception stays in separate channel. S-Agent 2.0 writes no controller and spends its design effort on closing the evidence loop at the interface: the models own perception enters the same scene as the tools measurements, every reading persists in scene memory that later calls query by name, and each reading comes back already interpreted in spatial language. General-purpose coding agents. Software-engineering agents such as SWE-agent [41] and OpenHands [36], developed against benchmarks such as SWE-bench [18], have matured into harnesses that supply shell, file system, code execution, long-horizon context management, and tool-calling loop that the backbone models are trained to follow. S-Agent 2.0 adopts such harness unchanged and adds perception as ordinary command-line tools, which is what lets the same method run under more than one of them (3.3). Two habits of these agents carry over 16 to spatial reasoning: viewing an image is an ordinary step in the same stream as the tool replies, and inspecting an output and revising it is reflex; together they are what joins the models own perception with the tools before reading is taken (3.4). Long-video and multi-view perception. Two families of methods supply the visual evidence these questions need. Frame-compression methods sample, retrieve, or summarize limited set of frames for long-context VLM, as in Video-LLaMA [48], LongVA [50], and [47], which keeps the context tractable at the risk of dropping the frames question turns on. Reconstructionfirst methods build an explicit 3D representation with multi-view geometry or feed-forward models such as VGGT [33] and Depth Anything 3 [20], which grounds the geometry well while paying the reconstruction cost on every question. Both families hand their output to the model as fixed context, leaving association across views and metric comparison to implicit reasoning. S-Agent 2.0 uses reconstruction and promptable segmentation backends of this kind as tool perception (2.3), with the agent deciding per question which of them to call and what to ground; what they measure and what the model registers itself land in one scene memory, and every reading comes back interpreted. Spatial reasoning benchmarks. Evaluation has moved from single-image probes such as BLINK [14] and EmbSpatial [13] to settings where the evidence is spread over many observations. MMSI-Bench [44] asks for evidence integrated across images of one scene, MindCube [34] probes the mental model built from few sparse views, and SPAR-Bench [49] spans hierarchy from metric perception to multi-view relational reasoning. For video, VSI-Bench [40] opened the setting, ReVSI [51] rebuilds its evaluation for more accurate assessment of 3D reasoning, and MMSI-Video-Bench [21] extends the MMSI setting to long videos with questions on spatial construction, motion, cross-video memory, and route planning. We evaluate on five of these (3.1). B. Toolkit interface The toolkit is one executable, python3 /app/perception.py <command> [flags], run from the agents shell like any other program. Every command reads and writes the scene memory of 2.2; its reply is JSON document on standard output, and every image it renders (segmentation overlays, top-down maps) is written to disk for the agent to open with its ordinary file viewer. The instruction is tutorial over these commands; this appendix lists the interface itself. Table 7 gives every command the agent is taught, grouped as in 2.3. Instance names. Every argument that refers to something in the scene is name. recon registers camera:f<N> for the camera of frame (position and orientation) and scene for the room centre. segment registers each prompts label as an instance (bed, desk); second, separate object under the same label becomes <label>_2, and f<N>:<label-or-id> names one frames view of an object, by label or by the id stamped on that frames overlay. add_instance names are chosen by the model. Two forms exist for compass only: camplane:f<N>, the image plane of camera N, and <name>plane, the plane fitted through an instances points. Positions and orientations for add_instance. position comes from one of three sources: at-map f<N>:PX,PY, pixel of the top-down map rendered from frame (height filled in from the reconstruction at that spot); view pixel X,Y, pixel of the original frame lifted to its 3D point; or at-camera N, the position of camera N. Removes those instances permanently. Returns the registry after the drop. No change. Returns each instances name, source, and whether it is oriented. No change. Returns straight-line, horizontal and vertical metres and conclusion. known calibrates scale. Returns, per target, forward_m, right_m, up_m in the observers frame (a cameras is its gravity-aligned ground heading), the three axis verdicts, the eight-way direction, and conclusion. No change. Returns each targets signed height above the reference along gravity, lowest-to-highest order, and conclusion. No change. For two cameras, returns the translation in the first cameras ground frame, the turn and tilt, and the path of the raw extrinsics; for one object in two frames, its shift as seen from the first camera, its rotation about the vertical and image_rotation in the image plane; each with conclusion. The anchor persists the compass mapping for later calls and maps. Returns the direction of each query, the eight compass words ranked by fit (nearest), and conclusion that, for an object-to-camera-plane query, states which side of the object that view sees. 18 literal gravity, or bev:f<N>:START:END, an arrow between two points on the map from frame N. facing is the upright shorthand (gravity fills the vertical, gives the heading), primary AXIS=V secondary AXIS=V the general form. second add_instance call with the same name and only orientation flags orients the existing instance in place. Reply anatomy. Every reply has the same shape: status flag, typed numeric fields in metres on the reconstructions own scale (a units field says whether the scale has been calibrated with known), and conclusion sentence per target that restates the measurement in spatial language. The side reply of the episode in Figure 4 (bottom right) reads, verbatim: $ python3 /app/perception.py side --observer sitting_person --of desk { "ok": true, "observer": "sitting_person", "sides": [ { } "target": "desk", "forward_m": 1.04, "right_m": -1.03, "up_m": 0.21, "front_or_behind": "front", "left_or_right": "left", "above_or_below": "above", "direction": "front-left", "conclusion": "desk is 1.04 in FRONT of sitting_person, 1.03 to its LEFT and 0.21 ABOVE it -- overall to its FRONT-LEFT" ], "units": "metres on the reconstructions own metric scale (uncalibrated)" } The executable also exposes lower-level commands (detect, measure, match, egomotion, gravity, render) that the instruction tells the agent not to use. C. Toolkit usage Table 8 counts, over every episode of three full-benchmark runs of S-Agent 2.0 under OpenHands, how often the agent issues each command of Table 7 and how often it opens each kind of image. Building the scene is universal: recon, segment and bev appear in over ninety percent of episodes on every run. The readouts follow the questions: MMSI-Bench, whose items ask about relations between views and viewpoints, draws side, motion and compass; ReVSI, whose items ask about distances, sizes and counts in video, draws distance and list_instance instead. The model perception interface is used in quarter to half of the episodes, and drop in fifth to two fifths, so registry edits are routine part of an episode rather than an exception. The lower-level commands the instruction reserves are called in under two percent of all calls. D. SpatialClaw with our readouts To separate what the readouts contribute from what the rest of the interface contributes, we add our readout commands to SpatialClaws kernel as plain functions and leave its harness, prompts and perception backends untouched. The transplanted set is distance, depth, side, elevation, motion and compass; each returns the same interpreted reply as in Table 7, packed into Python dictionary with the same keys (the numeric fields, the per-target conclusion and units), so the model reads it in its kernel exactly as our agent reads the JSON on standard output. list_instance is excluded because it reads the scene memory that SpatialClaw does not keep, and bev because SpatialClaw already renders top-down map of its own.
